heroTitle: Rehab is the first step. The years after it are the recovery.
heroBody: The 90 to 180 days most people spend in a facility is a very short period next to the years that follow. For many, adjusting to life afterwards is the harder part — the routine is gone and the old influences are back.
groupsParas: We strongly recommend that everyone in recovery attends support groups regularly, particularly in early sobriety. A group is people in recovery — and sometimes their families — meeting to discuss what they share, from how they first realised they needed to get sober to how a particular medication is affecting them.

The vast majority are 12-step programmes, which break recovery into steps all members follow. They are modelled on Alcoholics Anonymous — by research, the best known and most widely attended substance abuse group in the world.

groupBenefits.title: A judgement-free room
groupBenefits.body: Members feel understood, because everyone there has been in some version of the same place.

groupBenefits.title: Stability and people to fall back on
groupBenefits.body: A standing commitment in the week, and names you can call when a hard day arrives.

groupBenefits.title: Advice and information
groupBenefits.body: Practical, lived knowledge about what works — from people with no reason to sell you anything.

ourAftercareBody: We follow up on discharged clients, place people in the right support group and continue therapy where it is needed — plus practical strategies for managing cravings and stress.
timelineTitle: A continuous chain of small decisions.
timelineIntro: Sobriety is hardest to hold early on, and grows easier as new habits, relationships and routines form. This is roughly when to do what.

timeline.title: Build the scaffolding
steps: Develop a recovery plan with goals and how to reach them
Learn to recognise and handle negative impulses
Find healthy, supportive living arrangements
Establish a daily routine and schedule
Attend at least two support groups to find the best fit
Find a counsellor or therapist
Build a support system for when the urge appears
Bring in regular physical activity — and avoid taking on too much

timeline.title: Make it a habit
steps: Stay involved in support groups — at least weekly
Continue counselling or therapy, ideally weekly
Keep a recovery journal, including triggers and how you got past them
Discuss professional goals with a career counsellor

timeline.title: Repair and plan
steps: Begin repairing broken or damaged relationships
Develop short and long-term goals with a financial planner
Start focusing more on longer-term goals
Try new hobbies, then commit to one or two

timeline.title: Look outward
steps: Celebrate the milestones, especially six months and one year
Help others who are just beginning the road
Develop five and ten-year plans — personal, professional, financial
Seek out new motivation and new ways to occupy your time

relapseTitle: It happens to the most dedicated people in recovery. It is not the end of anything.
relapseBody: Some studies suggest the majority of people in recovery relapse at least briefly. Help is still here. Do not wait for the problem to get worse before you make the call — our relapse programme is two months, and we pick up where we left off.
